doc.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Professional start and leaving New Orleans
title: How King Oliver's rhythm section shaped Basie's
summary: Barker says the banjo gave way to a subtle bounce in rhythm guitar, which Bennie Moten and Count Basie took from King Oliver's band.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You got that from that, that rhythm section. Bennie Moten got that [expletive deleted] from King Oliver’s band. If you hear some of the King Oliver records, Canal Street Blues with Armstrong and Oliver, and you listen to Count Basie’s band, you’ll hear the same thing there which was done ten years earlier or maybe 15 years earlier.
So they got the influence from New Orleans.

That’s right, because they was . . . You see, people began to dance to a subtle sort of thing, not a blasting thing, but a bouncing. A heartbeat in the music. That’s what King Oliver had in his music with Baby Dodds and Bill Johnson. They had that old New Orleans funky sound. So that’s what you got. Later on, that’s what musicians all over the country tried to imitate, tried to get that sound. Basie had it, because he’s not a explosive piano player. He plays subtle piano, and he . . . honky tonk and a barrelhouse attitude, so you got that in the music. You can’t get that unless you have a barrelhouse attitude. You can’t play it.
